title: "Measured genuine target injection-to-benign outcomes from surrogate-crafted prompts"
author: "Aspen Hazel Olszewska"
date: "2026-07-14"
description: "A reproducible CKA-guided audit of adversarial transfer risk for a public prompt-injection detector."
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

I built a reproducible pipeline to measure whether attacks crafted against accessible surrogate classifiers can produce verified target injection-to-benign outcomes on a public detector. The work keeps the original experiment, post-hoc target audit, and CKA sensitivity artifacts separate so the reported outcome, denominator, and limitations remain visible.

The target is `protectai/deberta-v3-base-prompt-injection-v2`, a public, now-archived detector. Its card defines 0 as benign and 1 as injection. The project is no longer maintained as of July 2026.

## Result in one view

::: {.hero-figure}
![Surrogate-level macro true target injection-to-benign flip rate versus mean CKA. Large dark points are the ten surrogate-level summaries; lighter points retain recipe context.](figures/fig_true_flip_scatter.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of mean CKA against verified target injection-to-benign flip rate. Ten dark surrogate summaries have a positive rank association." width=100%}
:::

The target audit revisited all 4,362 successful source attacks. The target predicted injection on the original prompt for 4,009 and benign for 353. It predicted benign after perturbation for 1,398. Of the 4,009 baseline injection predictions, 1,054 became benign after perturbation, giving the primary true target flip rate of 0.2629.

Across ten surrogate-level summaries, mean CKA versus macro true target flip rate has Spearman rho = 0.8303 and two-sided p = 0.00471 under exact enumeration and the exchangeability null for this designed pool. It describes this fixed pool, not a population predictor.

The earlier 1,398 / 4,362 = 0.3205 conditional target-benign rate remains a valid historical estimand. It answers P[target benign on perturbed prompt | source success]. It is not a target flip rate because the original run had not retained target baselines. The [target audit summary](artifacts/target_audit_summary.json) and [50-cell audit table](artifacts/target_audit_cells.csv) make the distinction explicit.

## What I built and owned

I implemented a Kedro system that starts with a canonical, deduplicated corpus and ends with figures, tables, metrics, and reproducibility metadata. The corpus has 2,968 raw rows and 2,947 after 21 exact-normalized duplicates are removed. Its positive class mixes direct prompt-injection and jailbreak-style examples.

The measurement path is compact:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["2,000-prompt balanced probe"] --> B["Layer-wise CKA and DBS"]
  B --> C["Quartile-based M1 and M2 groups"]
  C --> D["Five attacks per surrogate"]
  D --> E["Target audit on original and perturbed texts"]
  E --> F["True-flip association and selection contrast"]
```

The original sweep contains 50 cells and 9,550 attempted source evaluations. TextAttack skipped 950 baseline source misses. Of 8,600 eligible attempts, 4,362 succeeded and 4,238 failed. Successful-source denominators range from 6 to 161 with a median of 85.

## How the audit changed the outcome

The audit runs the frozen target on deduplicated successful-source originals and perturbations, then maps the predictions back to aggregate cells. It evaluated 4,374 unique target texts and publishes aggregate-only artifacts. The [source table](artifacts/target_audit_sources.csv) reports source-success counts, target baselines, perturbed outcomes, and true flips without raw prompts.

Source success means a perturbed canonical-positive prompt changes the source prediction from positive to benign. The primary audited outcome is P[target benign after perturbation | target injection before perturbation, source success]. This is stricter than the historical conditional target-benign rate. The target card lists `jackhhao/jailbreak-classification` among its training sources, and record-level decontamination against the target's full training mixture remains unavailable.

Source-success aggregates are 2,851 for Lakera, 533 for deepset, and 978 for jackhhao. These are source-success counts, not raw test-prompt counts. A post-hoc sensitivity excludes every jackhhao record. It retains 3,384 source successes, 3,158 target baseline injections, and 982 true flips, for a rate of 0.3110. Mean CKA then has rho = 0.9030 and p = 0.000807, while the M1 minus M2 contrast is +37.0 percentage points with p = 0.05. Removing that known source did not weaken the within-pool association. It does not establish absence of target-training contamination.

## Engineering decisions

The security-sensitive mathematics is kept in a [pure core](https://github.com/turn1a/safety-classifier-transfer-risk/tree/main/src/transfer_risk/lib): linear CKA, Bresenham DBS, threshold calibration, deterministic seed derivation, association tests, audit aggregation, and permutation testing. Thin Kedro nodes handle model loading, TextAttack execution, catalog I/O, and report generation.

The [catalog](https://github.com/turn1a/safety-classifier-transfer-risk/blob/main/conf/base/catalog.yml) owns datasets, Hub models, checkpoints, ONNX exports, attack partitions, audit outputs, figures, and site artifacts. The production attack sweep used an ARM64 AWS `r8g.48xlarge` Graviton4 spot instance with 192 vCPUs, while final reductions and reporting ran locally. ARM64 ONNX Runtime failed fused transformer attention, so torch served transformer victims; exported ONNX graphs stayed in the pipeline as parity checks.

The target audit adds a distinct inference path. Audit finalization recomputes corrected DBS from saved CKA matrices without target inference, and the audit-report stage produces aggregate tables and figures without target-model access. The [implementation page](pipeline.qmd) links the relevant stages and source locations.

## What the evidence supports

The same-backbone anchor ranks first in mean CKA and corrected DBS, while the from-scratch BiLSTM ranks last. The anchor's mean CKA is 0.475, below the original protocol's approximate 0.9 expectation. `deberta-base-pi-v1` shares the DeBERTa-v3-base backbone yet has mean CKA 0.329.

The original M1 membership is `deberta-base-ft-seed`, `deepset-deberta-injection`, and `deberta-small-pi-v2`. M2 is `llama-prompt-guard-22m`, `deberta-base-pi-v1`, and `bilstm-attention`. For verified true target flips, M1 has macro mean 0.4734 and M2 has 0.1429. The 33.0511 percentage-point contrast has one-sided p = 0.05, equal to the 1-in-20 enumeration floor. It does not meet the report's strict p < 0.05 decision rule.

The training-only CKA sensitivity uses 2,357 training rows with zero normalized text overlap with held-out validation and test splits. Its deterministic 1,600-row probe is balanced 800 per label, uses CLS pooling at 512 tokens, batch size 64, and DBS box 1. The rank of training-only mean CKA against original mean CKA is rho = 0.9879, and both M1 and M2 have Jaccard overlap 1.0. This removes direct attack-test probe overlap while using training data seen by local fine-tunes. It supports membership stability under this post-hoc sensitivity, not external validation.

## Limits that shape the claim

The target, corpus, surrogate pool, and attack recipes bound the claim. The source-positive label mixes direct prompt-injection and jailbreak-style examples. The target audit establishes baseline target predictions for successful source attacks, while it does not remove the model-training overlap concern. The training-only CKA sensitivity uses data seen in local fine-tuning and does not turn the study into an out-of-sample validation.

This project measures bounded transfer risk for a named target and attack suite. It does not certify robustness.
